name: audit-logging.md
text:
# Audit logging for AI tool calls

## What to record
Every tool decision should be recorded: the calling identity, the tool, whether the call was allowed or denied, latency, and a correlation identifier that ties the record to the request. Arguments can be stored as a hash so the audit trail does not become a second copy of sensitive data.

## Tamper evidence
Chaining each record to the hash of the previous record makes the log tamper-evident: editing or deleting any record breaks every hash that follows. Periodic verification detects the break and identifies the first altered record.

## Shipping and retention
In AWS, audit records are shipped to CloudWatch Logs and archived to S3 with Object Lock for immutable retention. Security teams forward them to a SIEM for alerting on repeated denials or blocked egress attempts.

## Incident response
When an alert fires, responders use the correlation identifier to reconstruct which agent called which tool, with what result, and whether any outbound connection was attempted.

name: mcp-tool-security.md
text:
# Securing MCP tool servers

## Least privilege for agents
Each agent should receive only the scopes it needs. A research agent may search and answer from documents, while only an auditor identity may read audit status. Tools that are not listed in the authorization policy are denied by default.

## Prompt injection and tool misuse
Retrieved documents can contain instructions written by an attacker. Tool servers must treat model-generated tool arguments as untrusted input, validate them against a schema, bound sizes such as result counts, and never grant extra privileges because a prompt asks for them.

## Grounded answers
Answers should be built only from retrieved passages and cite the passage each claim comes from. A verifier can reject answers that cite sources that were never retrieved or that contain no citations at all.

## Transport protections
Streamable HTTP endpoints should validate the Host header to prevent DNS rebinding, require authentication on every request, and limit request body sizes.

name: mtls-identity.md
text:
# Mutual TLS and workload identity

## Why mutual TLS
Standard TLS proves the server's identity to the client. Mutual TLS also requires the client to present a certificate signed by a trusted certificate authority, so only enrolled workloads can open a connection at all. Connections without a valid client certificate fail during the TLS handshake, before any application code runs.

## Certificate authority
In AWS the private certificate authority is typically AWS Private CA. Certificates should be short-lived and rotated automatically; private keys stay on the workload and are never committed to source control.

## Enforcing client certificates
A TLS server must be explicitly configured to require client certificates. Many servers only request one, or accept connections without one, unless the verification mode is set to require a certificate. Integration tests should confirm that a client with no certificate, or with a certificate from an untrusted CA, is rejected.

## Combining mTLS with tokens
Mutual TLS authenticates the workload at the transport layer. Bearer tokens with scopes add application-level authorization, so a compromised but enrolled workload still cannot call tools outside its scopes.

name: secrets-and-keys.md
text:
# Secrets and key management

## Where secrets live
Application secrets belong in AWS Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store, encrypted with customer-managed KMS keys. Workloads read them at runtime through VPC endpoints using IAM roles, never from files committed to source control.

## Keys in git history
Deleting a committed private key in a new commit is not enough: the key remains in the repository history. The history must be rewritten to remove it, and the key must be considered compromised and rotated.

## Token storage
Services that validate static tokens should store only a hash of each token and compare hashes in constant time, so a leaked configuration file does not reveal usable credentials.

name: zero-egress.md
text:
# Zero-egress networking

## What zero egress means
A zero-egress workload has no route to the public internet. In AWS GovCloud this is achieved by placing workloads in private subnets with no internet gateway and no NAT gateway, so outbound traffic can only reach destinations inside the VPC.

## Reaching AWS services without the internet
Services such as S3, KMS, Secrets Manager, CloudWatch Logs and Bedrock are reached through VPC endpoints (AWS PrivateLink or gateway endpoints). Endpoint policies restrict which principals and resources each endpoint can be used for.

## Defense in depth inside the application
Network controls can be misconfigured, so the application should also refuse outbound connections it does not expect. An in-process allowlist that checks every socket connect turns an accidental or prompt-injected outbound call into a logged, blocked event instead of a data leak.

## Model hosting under zero egress
Language models must run inside the boundary: a self-hosted model on private compute, or a managed model service reached through a VPC endpoint. Prompts and retrieved documents must never be sent to a public API.
